title: Interview journal — Anaïs Fernandez (reflective loop notes)
content:
Quick context:
- Candidate: Anaïs Fernandez — applied for Senior Runtime Engineer. Remote, based in Lisbon.
- Loop format: 90 minutes + 30 minutes async take-home review. Pair-programming on a simplified KV cache eviction problem, systems design discussion about routing & fallback policies, and a short behavioral conversation.

My immediate gut reaction (raw):
- Thoughtful, pauses to outline before jumping in — good mental modeling.
- Uses whiteboard to map state transitions for KV cache and TTL; sketching was tidy and pragmatic rather than academic.
- Slightly defensive when challenged on trade-offs (latency vs memory), but recovered after clarifying assumptions.
- Took ownership of missed edge-case in pair session quickly; debugged with targeted tests.

Detailed notes by segment:
1) Warm intro (5–10m)
- Friendly, quick rapport. Mentioned prior infra work at mid-size ML infra org.
- Emphasized experience with cost/perf tradeoffs and quantization pipelines (relevant to our Optimize work).

2) Pair-programming (40m) — KV cache eviction (simulated environment)
- Approach: Asked clarifying Qs about workload distribution (hot keys vs long tails). Good start.
- Chose LRU variant with frequency heuristic (LFU-lite) and a simple admission policy.
- Implementation style: clear variable names, incremental tests. Preferred defensive checks (null guards) — aligns with production ops mindset.
- Missed an eviction race in concurrent access scenario initially. After I pointed it out, they proposed a lock-striping approach to reduce contention and sketched how eventual consistency would look.
- Tradeoffs: highlighted that strict correctness under heavy concurrency would require heavier locking or compare-and-swap loops; recommended sharded counters + background rebalancer as a practical compromise.
- Communication: explained decisions, but sometimes used jargon without quick translation for non-IC reviewers. Suggest coaching to tailor language in cross-functional discussions.

3) System design (30m) — routing & fallback policies for multi-variant models
- Strength: thought through policies (latency-SLO-first vs cost-first) and multi-tier fallbacks. Proposed a routing matrix keyed on request type, customer tier, and observed tail latency.
- Proposed dynamic fallback that uses exponential backoff for degrading model variants and keeps a short circuit if errors exceed threshold. Nice practical details.
- Less confident about metrics instrumentation: proposed basic histograms, but struggled to explain how to tie quality regressions to rollout decisions (no mention of prompt sets/evals until I prompted).
- Brought up cache-coherence concerns for prefix caching across replicas — suggested bloom filters + versioned prefixes to avoid stale reads. That felt creative and pragmatic.

4) Behavioral / culture fit (15m)
- Values: emphasizes shipping, on-call experience, and balancing reliability with iteration.
- Examples: described a postmortem where they introduced a fallback that decreased customer impact by ~30% — good concrete impact language.
- Mentoring: has experience coaching juniors; enjoys pair programming.
- Red flag?: When asked about trade-offs they've lost, they framed some failures as "learning opportunities" but downplayed stakeholder communication hiccups. Would like to probe async communication/ stakeholder management in follow-up.

Take-home review (async) — short Python microservice + tests:
- Code was generally clean, but the API surface had an undocumented edge case where malformed metadata could cause 500. They wrote tests but missed malformed metadata test. Left a note in the PR acknowledging that and included a short fix plan.
- Tests used property-based style instead of exhaustive cases (I liked that approach but it missed a couple of boundary inputs).

Scorecard (my quick, out-of-10 impressions; use as conversation starter):
- Technical depth (systems): 8/10 — solid grounding, pragmatic tradeoffs, good design heuristics.
- Concurrency & correctness: 6.5/10 — understands problems well, needs a nudge on low-level concurrency patterns under stress.
- Communication: 7/10 — clear with engineers, could be more accessible for PMs/CS.
- Product sense / ops focus: 8/10 — strong awareness of customer impact and SLOs.
- Culture / team fit: 7.5/10 — collaborative, enjoys coaching; some follow-up needed on cross-team comms.

Signals to hire (pros):
- Practical, production-aware engineering. Knows cost/latency tradeoffs which matters for Redwood Optimize and serving runtime.
- Comfortable with on-call and postmortem culture; has measurable impact examples.
- Approaches problems with incremental delivery + tests.

Concerns / risks (cons):
- Occasionally leans on higher-level heuristics without immediately accounting for rare concurrency edge cases. Might need a peer with low-level concurrency expertise early in pairing.
- Slight tendency to default to technical jargon in cross-functional conversations — may slow stakeholder alignment unless coached.

Suggested follow-ups / interview plan changes:
- Small practical exercise focused on concurrency hazards: e.g., design a sharded counter with compare-and-swap and show how to avoid ABA/overflow issues. Watch for lock-free thinking vs pragmatic sharding.
- Ask for an example where they had to escalate a technical decision to leadership and how they framed the trade-offs. Probe communication.
- Pair them with someone from Optimize or Serving Runtime who can take deeper concurrency questions.

Compensation / leveling note (tentative):
- Level: Senior (IC4/IC5 depending on breadth). Has areas to grow in low-level concurrency but strong product/ops instincts.
- Comp band: suggest mid-range for Senior IC or low-range Staff depending on prior org/title & systemic impact evidence.

Admin notes / next steps:
- Share these raw notes with Priya & Marcus; recommend scheduling a 30m follow-up specifically for concurrency deep-dive.
- Candidate is available for a follow-up next week midday CET.
- I left comments on their PR (linked above) with suggested test cases and a small patch.

Random scratch bullets (things I may forget):
- Loved their bloom-filter idea for prefix caching evictions. Could be useful to inspire an infra spike.
- Mentioned previous work on quantization savings — cross-link to Optimize team to see fit.
- Ask about their experience with KMS/HSM (brought up briefly when discussing Private deployments).

Bottom line (one-liner):
- Anaïs is a strong Senior-level candidate with practical production sensibilities and solid design instincts; recommend a focused follow-up on concurrency correctness and cross-team communication examples before final decision.
